population.note: FICTIONAL. Arithmetic: 37.5% ever-used minus 28.0% current = 9.5% of adults who used and are off now. Age check: 0.20×17 + 0.33×28.5 + 0.24×39 + 0.23×25 = 3.4 + 9.4 + 9.4 + 5.75 ≈ 27.9. Income thirds average ~27.7, bracketing the national figure. 28.0% of ~274M adults is ~76.7M users, up ~23M. drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. Next-gen driver realised through an existing product in a new form. Lilly filed a high-dose retatrutide sNDA in mid-2032 on the TRIUMPH programme's 12 mg arms, and the FDA approved the 12 mg maintenance dose in Mar 2033 at ~28–29% mean weight loss at 80 weeks, labelled with lean-mass, heart-rate and dysaesthesia language and a resistance-training counselling statement. No new triple agonist molecule was approved. Others are in phase 3 in China and the US, and none has a US filing. Oral semaglutide for AUD, filed Jan 2032, was approved Aug 2033. Compulsion use is realised off-label: a Novo phase 3 in gambling disorder began in 2033 and reads out no earlier than 2036, so there is no compulsion indication. Longevity is off-label only and no ageing indication exists. Bimagrumab, filed Jul 2032, was approved Jun 2034 as an adjunct to incretin therapy in adults 18+ with obesity, after modest lean-mass data. Tirzepatide's dementia confirmatory trial reads out 2035, and Lilly has not refiled the non-CVD extension. Implants remain in phase 1–2 and are not on the market. No oral matches tirzepatide. US net prices drift down 3–5% a year and brands hold ~$150–300 cash.

safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class warning (Jul 2028) retained; DXA code in use; bimagrumab approved as an adjunct; resistance-training statements on retatrutide (incl. 12 mg) and amycretin labels.

It confirmed an association at weight-loss doses, could not separate it from confounding, and had too little low-dose exposure to say anything about calm, longevity or Reset plans.

The Swedish registry ARFID HR is unchanged at ~1.8. Final adult height is still unknown.

The longevity segment created a new premium aisle, with 'metabolic' fibre, creatine and peptide-adjacent supplements. Pea protein is still tight.

Lifestyle spending accounts now reimburse calm and Reset platform fees at ~19% of large employers, which looks like a wellness perk rather than drug coverage. Part D premiums rose again for 2034. pharma.state: Lilly regained momentum with retatrutide 12 mg among cash-paying upper-income users. Novo leans on orals, the AUD label and the low-dose cash market it does not advertise. Amgen's MariTide holds employer tracks. Counterfeit-defence and litigation spending runs above $1B a year across the four. Indian and Chinese makers dominate global volume. US sportsbook operators cite 'pharmacological headwinds' in investor calls, which are now a pharma story too.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: The body still reads as income and payment route, and now also as motive. Lean, scanned and muscled means covered and coached. Lean but already thin before the drug, with a daily pill, means the longevity tier: people who were never obese and take it for their bloodwork. Thin, soft and bruised monthly means the employer track. Regained, or visibly mid-cycle, means gray market and a seizure or bad batch. A child's growth chart and a parent's DXA sit side by side as upper-tier status documents.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: In Austin and Charlotte the elite marker has moved from weight to biomarkers: HbA1c, lean-mass percentage, 'biological age' on a clinic printout. 'Off-drug lean' still impresses, but the newest boast is 'never needed it, take it anyway'. Along the Columbus logistics corridor, the track body is standard issue among shift leads. In Memphis and the Mississippi Delta, gray 'reta' vials brought surgical-grade losses to people who could never have paid $299, along with hypoglycaemia scares and the fastest regains in the country. In the eleven ban states, upper-income parents had already stopped prepubertal starts. The ban mostly removed Medicaid-covered children who had started late.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are shorter and more often protein-led. Holiday tables in high-density zips feature 'tasting' portions. The Bread Alone fasting network claims ~800 congregations. School weight reporting was dropped in several states as part of the same 2034 packages that set the age limits.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: 'Lean-mass verified' and 'biomarker verified' are premium app tiers. 'Reset' badges signal someone who has quit betting or porn on a plan, and they are read as either reliability or flatness. Couples negotiate around shot dates and calm-plan schedules. Therapists report partners matched on a calm plan presenting together with 'nothing wrong, nothing happening'.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: In the upper tier, appetite, craving, the urge to bet and the urge to buy are all classed as noise that a subscription manages. In lower-income communities appetite signals lost access or a seized package, and it is defended as pride. Unmuted now organises around sportsbook and shopping 'Reset' marketing as much as food. The MAHA wing claimed the 2034 age bans as its victory, and fat-acceptance revivalists stay apart from both.

Their anhedonia rate is unmeasured; the FDA observational study had too little low-dose exposure. ~7.4M workers are in adherence-verified tracks, and LSAs at ~19% of large employers reimburse calm and Reset platform fees.
interior_life.framing: Employers and benefit brokers call it 'steadiness' and 'regulation'. Platforms, barred from mood claims after the 2034 consent orders, now say 'metabolic balance' and let reviews do the rest. Clinicians call it a dose-related side effect. Unmuted calls it a workplace sedative paid out of the wellness budget.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Adherence now tracks employment more tightly. At Columbus-corridor 3PLs and national call-centre operators, track enrollees are about twice as likely to be promoted to shift lead in internal data obtained by reporters. Vendors sell 'focus cohort' attrition analytics showing calm-plan users quit less. One of the two 2031 EEOC ADA charges was dismissed and the other received a right-to-sue letter; a federal suit in the Southern District of Ohio is pending. Upper-tier staff list 'Reset' alongside sleep tracking in performance reviews, voluntarily.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Sportsbook handle per active account is down ~14% from 2032 in high-density user states, and operators lobby against Reset plan advertising while it is still running. 'Off' memoir and 'Reset' confession videos compete. Ambient series and long-form slow games are programmed for the calm segment. Unmuted off nights have spread to Cleveland and Birmingham. Stand-up comedians now have the flat audience as a genre.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Desire mismatch remains the leading complaint at couples' practices. The Reset tier added a new pattern: a partner who quit porn or gambling on a plan, whose spouse cannot tell whether they have changed or just been turned down. Shared calm plans normalise low-conflict, low-intensity marriages.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The restriction coalition was MAHA legislators plus progressive consumer advocates. It passed under-12 bans and telehealth prescribing rules in eleven states, and it pushed the FTC–FDA consent orders, but it never touched employer adherence premiums, where business lobbies held the line. Gaming industry money backed advertising limits on Reset plans. 'Sedated electorate' claims still lack turnout evidence. Medicated and regained voters sort further by zip code.

state.regulatory_posture: Permissive on products, restrictive on marketing and the young. The FDA approved retatrutide 12 mg, oral semaglutide for AUD and bimagrumab. In 2034 the FTC and FDA signed consent orders with Level and three other platforms barring calm, focus and compulsion claims. Eleven states (Texas, Florida, Louisiana, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Indiana, Ohio, Utah, Missouri, West Virginia) enacted under-12 bans on weight-indication prescribing. Seven of them also require an in-person visit within 12 months for any incretin prescribed to adults with BMI under 27 without a qualifying diagnosis, a de facto prescribing cap on telehealth longevity use. Six banned social-media advertising of off-label incretin uses. Congress passed nothing.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: None new. TrumpRx operates on manufacturer-set prices. The Medicare Bridge pilot was not revived. The 2027 tri-agency 30% wellness guidance stands.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Unchanged in law, deeper in practice. Clinic administration records, PBM fills, telehealth mood check-ins and now LSA reimbursement claims flow to wellness vendors under consent. Brokers sell de-identified 'focus' and 'Reset' cohort analytics to employers. Two state Medicaid programmes still condition coverage on adherence and BMI progress.
state.workforce_or_military: TRICARE is unchanged. The Army recruit oral pilot continues. In 2033 DOT issued interpretive guidance treating incretins as non-disqualifying for commercial drivers, including AUD and off-label calm use, provided they are prescribed and disclosed. That leaves gray-market use undisclosed by definition.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: India and China supply ~70% of world incretin volume. After the Nov 2033 insulin-pen deaths, India agreed to require export registration for B2C pharmaceutical parcels (effective 2035), with no CBP mail agreement. Chinese 'reta' supply runs through research-peptide fronts that the import alerts name but cannot track. Beijing protested the expanded alerts. The US cash-to-Indian-generic gap is ~40–60×.

open_tensions: Restriction hit the licensed channel, not the drug. State BMI floors and advertising bans pushed longevity and calm users toward gray vials in the same year that counterfeit insulin pens killed nineteen microdosers. Gray use has doubled to 15.4 million and India's parcel registration does not start until 2035.

Employers do not cover weight drugs any more broadly than before, but they do reimburse calm and Reset fees and promote people with complete adherence records. The Ohio lawsuit will test whether preferring the steady is disability discrimination, while the 30% premium guidance still stands.

The eleven-state under-12 ban mostly removed Medicaid children who had started late, while the children already on drug in other states still have no final adult height data.

prose.headline: Twenty-Eight Percent and Steady: America Medicates Its Cravings, Its Bets and Its Bloodwork, and the Boss Prefers It That Way
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2034 more than one American adult in four takes an incretin drug, about seventy-seven million people, and nearly two in five have tried one. Coverage did not cause the jump: employers who pay for weight loss slipped from 30 to 29 percent, and Medicare still reaches people only through heart, kidney, diabetes, sleep-apnoea and narrow dementia codes. The new users came through cash and through the mail, and many of them were never obese.

The largest new market is bloodwork. Longevity clinics in Austin, Miami and Scottsdale made low-dose semaglutide a standard line on the lab panel, and about nine million adults without obesity now pay for 'metabolic health' plans. Behind them is a quieter market. After the FDA approved oral semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in August 2033, telehealth companies began selling the same pill as a 'Reset' for sports betting, online shopping and screens. More than a million and a half people subscribe. The calm and focus plans that began in 2031 have tripled.

Prices fell as manufacturers chose. MariTide is $219 a month in cash, the Wegovy pill $179 at maintenance, and starting pills still $149. In March 2033 Lilly won approval for a 12 mg retatrutide dose that takes off about 29 percent of body weight, close to surgery, for $299. The list price on the Wegovy box is still $1,349.

The mail carries everything the pharmacies do not. Some fifteen million Americans use imported or counterfeit product, double the number two years ago. Indian semaglutide is a few dollars a vial, and Chinese 'reta' vials sold as research peptides carry anything from nothing to three times the label. In November 2033 counterfeit pens turned out to contain insulin. About eleven hundred people went to emergency rooms with collapsing blood sugar and nineteen died, most of them healthy microdosers who did not know what low blood sugar felt like.

The state finally acted, and mostly at the edges. Eleven states banned weight-loss prescribing for children under twelve, building on the 2032 growth data that showed children who started early growing more slowly. Seven of those states require an in-person visit before a telehealth doctor can prescribe to a lean adult. Federal regulators made four platforms stop promising calm or freedom from compulsion. The platforms now say 'balance' and let customer reviews say the rest. Some lean customers who lost easy prescriptions bought vials instead. Congress did nothing, and the rule letting employers charge up to 30 percent more to workers whose adherence is not verified still stands.

Employers found their own use for the drugs. About one large employer in five now reimburses calm or Reset subscription fees as a lifestyle perk, which is not the same as covering the drug. Seven and a half million workers are in monitored tracks. At freight hubs and call centres, internal numbers obtained by reporters show enrollees promoted to shift lead at twice the rate of everyone else. A former agent is suing in Ohio. Vendors sell analytics showing that calm workers quit less.

Bodies keep sorting. In Charlotte the boast is a biological-age printout. On the Columbus freight corridor shift leads carry the monthly clinic bruise. In Memphis, gray retatrutide gave surgical-grade losses to people who could never pay $299, along with the fastest regains in the country once a package was seized. Sportsbook operators report bettors wagering less per account. Spirits volumes are down a sixth. Couples' therapists describe marriages with nothing wrong and nothing happening. Nothing in the country looks broken.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Dana Pruitt clocks in at the Groveport distribution centre at 5:40 and goes straight to the plant clinic, because the first Tuesday is shot day. The nurse, Kemi, swabs her belly, gives the MariTide, and taps the tablet. Somewhere a premium stays thirty percent lower.

'Scale's due,' Kemi says. The InBody prints out. Lean mass down a point. Kemi circles it and writes BAND CLASS? and Dana nods the way she always nods.

At the 6:00 huddle the board shows her team green on steadiness. Two of her pickers are on calm plans. The company reimburses the platform fee, and the pills are $179 on TrumpRx. Jalen isn't, and everyone can tell, because he laughs too loud and argues about routes. He is good at routes.

On break she deletes the sportsbook app again. It keeps reinstalling from the cloud.

Her brother Ray texts a photo from Memphis: a carton from a Telegram seller, six vials, REAL RETA in marker. Down 40 lbs, he writes. She types 'the insulin ones' and deletes it and sends a thumbs-up.

At pickup, her son Owen, ten, is taller than the boy next to him for the first time. Ohio's ban took him off liraglutide in July, and the pediatrician said it didn't matter much either way, which is what she says about most things.

At dinner her husband Mike, off Zepbound since his layoff, eats a second plate fast and watches her not finishing hers.

'You're quiet,' he says.

'I'm fine,' she says, and means it, and that's the part she can't explain.

prose.headline: The Pill Caught Up, the Pen Got Pricier, and Your Shoulders Now Tell Everyone What You Earn
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2034 almost three American adults in ten are on an incretin drug. Whether someone is on it no longer tells you much. What tells you something is the shape the drug left behind. Across a Scottsdale brunch table or a Buckhead gym floor, trained shoulders and a steady waist mean a coached regimen: twelve milligrams of Lilly's triple agonist or Amgen's new monthly shot, a scan every year, a trainer who knows bone. On the west side of Phoenix or in Dayton, a soft middle over thin arms means something else. It means kiosk weigh-ins, a plan that cut you off, a pen bought in a parking lot. The molecules are the same and the bodies are different.

The gap widened because prices went up, which almost nobody had planned for. Generic semaglutide was supposed to reach American shelves in 2033. Instead the FDA issued a warning letter to the company that held the first right to launch, and under the law's 180-day rule nobody else could launch either. Rival generics now wait for 2035. That summer Novo recalled millions of pens over sterility failures, and injectable semaglutide went into shortage for five months. When supply returned, the old price commitments had quietly expired, and Novo and Lilly added about fifty dollars a month to maintenance prices. Medicare did not move, because its $199 rate and $50 copay are fixed in statute. So the increase fell on employers, cash buyers and everyone in between.

Employers answered with conditions. Most covering plans were already gated by weight loss and adherence. Now a growing share also require a year on the job before the drug is covered, and they price premiums off verified kiosk weights. Benefits consultants call it metabolic tenure. Warehouse workers call it waiting to vest. There was no new law and no new federal rule. The continuation standard that governs Medicare and thirty-one state Medicaid programmes is exactly what it was in 2032.

The people priced out did not stop. They went abroad by parcel. About seven million Americans now use imported or counterfeit product, nearly double the 2032 figure: Indian generic pens at twenty or thirty dollars, Chinese 'research' vials of drugs the FDA has not cleared at those doses. In November 2033 a run of contaminated vials sent about four hundred people to hospital across six Southeastern states and killed eleven. Poison-centre calls are up by more than two-thirds. Harm-reduction volunteers now circulate lot-number blacklists on Telegram, and the authentication bill is still stuck in committee.

In February the needle stopped being necessary for most people. A fifty-milligram Wegovy pill matched the weekly injection head to head, and millions switched, many of them shortage refugees. The pill matches the shot most people use, not the strongest ones, so top-tier results still come from a pen. Within weeks counterfeiters were pressing tablets.

In May the eye warning arrived. After years of conflicting studies, the FDA put a class warning for optic-nerve stroke on every GLP-1 product, at a relative risk of about 1.7. At this scale that means roughly two thousand excess cases a year, mostly partial and permanent vision loss in one eye. The warning applies to every box, including the four and a half million 'Quiet' and 'Even' subscribers who take a low dose for calm and focus with no weight problem at all. Their onboarding screen now shows the eye warning just under the word calm. Nobody has measured what the drug does to them, which is also true of their pleasure.

The bone wave keeps rising with the older user base, now about fifteen thousand excess hip fractures a year, billed to a part of Medicare that does not pay for the drug. Everyone is waiting for 2035 again.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
At 5:40 Marisol Ortega holds the pen under the kitchen light and reads the lot number twice. The Maryvale Telegram list has forty-one flagged batches since November. Hers isn't on it. Twenty-eight dollars, from a woman who drives up from Nogales on Thursdays. She injects beside her navel and checks the box for the eye leaflet. Hers is printed in Hindi.

She switched agencies in March for two dollars more an hour. The new plan covers the drug after twelve months. September, if she lasts.

By eight she is in Arcadia, unpacking Mrs. Halvorsen's mail-order box: the new pill, a Part D sticker, fifty dollars, an orange insert about sudden blurring. Mrs. Halvorsen is eighty-one and tells her the pill is easier than the pen they took away last summer. Marisol cuts the toast into strips and pours the fortified milk.

At eleven the DEXA van is parked at the Lutheran church. Mrs. Halvorsen's scan is due. Marisol wheels her across the lot and waits on a folding chair beside a man in a golf shirt whose shoulders fill it. His trainer is texting him about his lean-mass number.

On the drive home she stops at the Fry's kiosk out of habit. She steps on, but there is no plan for it to report to. The screen thanks her anyway.

Her daughter calls from Tucson. Her company's plan covers Zepbound now, with a coach. Come visit, Mami, we'll go to the gym.

Marisol says Sunday, maybe. She buys the big tub of discount protein, and on the way to the car she looks at her arms in the window.

prose.headline: The Pill Caught Up. The Vials Got Expensive. And Now Your Nine-Year-Old Qualifies.
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2034 roughly one American adult in four takes an incretin drug, about sixty-eight million people, and more than a third have tried one. The rise was faster than in any earlier two years, and it rests on three things that happened in Washington and one in a laboratory.

The laboratory result was a pill. In February 2034 the FDA approved oral amycretin, Novo's daily tablet, which in its phase 3 trial took off about a fifth of body weight, as much as the injectables that had defined the decade. People who would never inject now swallow, and the pill is now the dominant route. It costs about $449 a month in cash and sits behind prior authorisation everywhere else. The Wegovy starting pill is still $149 through TrumpRx. Six million people now stay on that starting dose indefinitely because it is what they can afford, a regimen nobody has studied.

The first Washington change was a label. In January 2033 the Wegovy pill was approved for alcohol use disorder. Because that is not a weight-loss use, Medicaid has to cover it, and so does Medicare, which still pays nothing for weight alone. Bourbon country noticed first. Around Bardstown the distilleries cut shifts, and in Dayton the bars hold pill nights. The telehealth calm platforms noticed too. They now screen every new subscriber for drinking, and about a third of their 2.4 million customers are written on the alcohol label, which lets the companies advertise freedom from craving to drinkers. CMS has begun auditing the diagnoses.

The second was a tariff. In April 2033 a 100 percent duty on Chinese and Indian peptide drugs came into force, along with an Indian promise to check exports to American mailboxes. The Indian vial that cost forty dollars now costs a hundred and forty. About 1.7 million people left the gray market. Half went to the $149 pill and half stopped, and in Memphis and the Delta the regain is visible on the street. People there call it the hunger tax. The trade did not end. Smuggled powder is now refilled into vials in back rooms in Mississippi and Alabama, and this year a cluster of infections from those vials killed three people.

The third was a condition. The federal employee health programme now pays for weight drugs only for members who prove they take them and lose five percent in six months. Most employers that still cover the drugs do the same. Coverage technically rose, to a third of employers, but it now comes with a log, a scan and a premium tier that drops if the log goes quiet. Nine and a half million workers live inside those tracks.

The scandal landed in the middle of all this. In June 2033 documents unsealed in the federal litigation showed Novo's own safety staff had flagged a pancreatic warning sign in 2027, and it reached regulators only as rows in a table. Novo set aside six billion dollars, its medical chief resigned, and the lawsuits over stomach paralysis and pancreatic failure passed ninety thousand. Novo's new pill is still the fastest launch in the class.

Then the children. In February 2034 weekly semaglutide was approved for six-to-eleven-year-olds, with the same instruction as before: measure height every six months and screen for disordered eating. The trial showed the same slower growth. Parents in Bethesda and Plano mostly declined and bought family strength classes. Most new starts are Medicaid children, covered under federal rules for children's medical necessity. In May sixty thousand people rallied on the Mall under the banner Let Them Grow. No state passed anything. From a distance the country looks steadier, drinks less and eats less. Up close it is being logged.

Lorna Pruitt sets her alarm for 5:10 so she can take the pill thirty minutes before coffee, with four ounces of water and nothing else. It is the $149 starting dose. It has been the $149 starting dose for fourteen months, since the Mumbai seller's vials went to a hundred and forty-five and then stopped coming. Her jeans have stopped getting looser. They have not started getting tighter, and that is what she is paying for.

At the bus depot on Lamar she runs dispatch. A driver named Curtis leans in the window and asks if the drinking pill shows up on a drug test. She tells him to ask the examiner, because that is what the memo says. He says his cousin got it free through TennCare. She says good for his cousin.

At lunch she eats half a turkey sandwich and wraps the rest for later. Later she won't eat it.

At four she picks up Kiara, who is ten, from the clinic on Elvis Presley Boulevard. The nurse measured her again, four feet six and a quarter. They wrote it on the chart, and Kiara asked to see the line. It bends a little. Kiara gets the shot on Sundays. TennCare pays. The nurse said the line is still inside the band.

At home her husband has the news on: people on the Mall holding signs with children's height charts. Kiara watches for a minute and asks if those are kids like her.

Lorna says no, those are other kids, and turns it to the cooking channel, and Kiara watches a woman make bread.
